title: I'm Starting to Think We Can't Save Students From AI
author: Sharkey, Sydney
summary: The more I think about my place as an educator, a media literacy scholar, and simply as a human being trying to navigate the rise of artificial intelligence, the more I find myself returning to an idea rooted in my studies as a media literacy scholar: the protectionist approach. In media literacy scholarship, the protectionist approach was one of the earliest paradigms. Emerging in the mid-twentieth century alongside concerns about television, film, and mass media, it positioned audiences, especially children, as passive recipients who needed to be shielded from harmful messages. The assumption was pretty straightforward. The media were powerful, audiences were vulnerable, and education's job was to protect them. Sydney Sullivan, PhD is a reader-supported publication. Later, critical media literacy pushed even further, asking students not only to interpret media but to question who creates it, whose interests it serves, and how systems of power shape what we see. Instead of treating students as empty vessels waiting to be filled with the "right" answers, critical media literacy assumes they possess agency. They are capable of questioning, resisting, creating, and making informed decisions for themselves. That belief has become foundational to my own teaching. I've never wanted to rule my classroom with an iron fist. I've never believed education works through surveillance or punishment. The idea that we can--or should--protect people from every harmful technology starts to feel a little too close to Orwell's 1984 for my comfort. If students never have opportunities to exercise judgment, are we actually teaching them to think critically? And yet...The classroom has become the place where my philosophy collides with reality. Can I really expect students to stop using AI simply because I teach them about its ethical, environmental, and cognitive implications? Can I assign research on declining critical thinking, discuss the environmental costs of massive data centers, or facilitate conversations about authorship and learning, and expect students to respond, "You're right, Dr. Sharkey. I'll never use ChatGPT again." I'm not naive enough to think yes. Students are exhausted. They're juggling work, caregiving responsibilities, anxiety, financial stress, and impossible schedules. Sometimes they're sick. Sometimes they're overwhelmed. Other times, maybe they are genuinely just being lazy. No matter the excuse--valid or invalid--convenience is powerful, and AI offers convenience in abundance. Lately I've found myself thinking a lot about Sarah Wilson 's newest book, Eat the Stars and her writing on climate grief. You'll have to read it, it's a good cry--both happy and sad. She argues that hope, at least as we usually define it, can become its own kind of trap. We keep waiting for evidence that everything will be okay before we decide to act. But there comes a point when certainty disappears and there is a strange relief in accepting that we may not be able to fix everything. Oddly enough, I've begun wondering if AI in education demands a similar kind of thinking. Not hopelessness in the sense of giving up, but in the sense of relinquishing the illusion that I can control every outcome. As a first-generation college student, education changed my life. It gave me confidence when I had very little. It taught me how to think, not just what to think. It gave me purpose. It made democracy feel personal because it taught me that ideas matter and that my voice mattered too. That belief is still at the center of why I teach. But maybe my responsibility isn't to save every student from AI. Years ago, when I first started teaching, a mentor told me something I've thought about often: Focus on the good ones. At the time, I hated that advice. It sounded elitist and dismissive of students who struggle. I was one of those students. Plenty of brilliant people don't arrive in college polished or confident or motivated every single semester. But over the years, I've tweaked that advice to: Focus on the ones who care. There are still so many students who are still willing to wrestle with difficult questions. Students who are curious enough to revise, to reflect, to wonder whether outsourcing their thinking is actually costing them something. I can't police every suspicious em dash. I can't investigate every oddly polished paragraph or every sentence that begins, "It's not that we're seeing this. It's actually that." I also can't build an educational philosophy around suspicion. However, I can certainly create classrooms where thinking is valued, where reflection feels worthwhile, and where students encounter ideas strong enough to make them pause before asking AI to do the thinking for them. Critical media literacy has always argued that education isn't about controlling people. It's about helping them develop the capacity to choose. Maybe AI hasn't changed that as much as I thought. It's simply made the stakes of choice impossible to ignore. -Dr. Sydney Sydney Sullivan, PhD is a reader-supported publication.
